figures.before: What MEP Means and Why Coordination Is the Single Biggest Driver of Commercial Construction Cost Overruns
figures.alt: Commercial interior rough-in with coordinated HVAC ductwork, sprinkler mains, conduit racks, cable tray, piping, and support systems before drywall
figures.caption: MEP coordination is where spatial design becomes buildable work. Ducts, pipe, conduit, controls, equipment, supports, access, ceilings, structure, and fire protection all have to occupy the same building without blocking one another.

figures.before: The 7 MEP Systems in a Complex Commercial Building
figures.alt: Commercial restroom under construction with accessible clearances, wall backing, plumbing rough-ins, and metal-stud framing
figures.caption: The individual systems become real at the rough-in stage. Plumbing, electrical, ventilation, controls, fire protection, framing, backing, finishes, access, and inspection requirements all need a coordinated location.

figures.before: MEP Inspection Sequencing: Why Rough-In Must Be Approved Before Drywall
figures.alt: Residential renovation rough-in inspected with open framing, routed services, and a clean protected work area
figures.caption: Rough-in approval protects the project from closing a wall or ceiling around work that has not been verified. It depends on complete installation, access, records, inspection timing, and a clean handoff to the next phase.
